job.style: a short story with Indian characters in everyday life

passage: Aarav and his grandfather sat on their balcony in Delhi, watching the sunset. Aarav asked, 'Dadu, does the Sun travel behind the Earth to hide at night?' His grandfather smiled and explained that the Earth spins on its own invisible axis, which causes day and night. He clarified that this axis is just an imaginary line, not a physical pole. Aarav then asked about the changing weather. 'Is it summer because we are closer to the Sun?' he wondered. Dadu shook his head, explaining that seasons change due to the Earth's tilt and its revolution around the Sun, not because of the distance. He added that the Earth takes about 365 and a quarter days to complete one orbit. To keep our calendar accurate, we add an extra day to February every four years, which we call a leap year. Aarav realized that the Earth is a complex, moving home. He felt amazed thinking about the planet spinning silently while they sat there. The cool evening breeze reminded him that even though the Earth is always in motion, they feel perfectly still on its surface. It was a beautiful lesson about the world they live in.

items.evidence: He clarified that this axis is just an imaginary line, not a physical pole.
items.q: Aarav wants to touch the Earth's axis. Why can he not do this?
options: It is only an imagined line
It is a pole that is too tall
It is covered by the oceans
items.explain: Dadu said the axis is just an imaginary line, not a physical pole, so nobody can touch it.

wrong.why: thinks the axis is a real object inside Earth
thinks the axis is a real pole that is too big
guesses a hiding place without using the passage

items.evidence: His grandfather smiled and explained that the Earth spins on its own invisible axis, which causes day and night.
items.q: How does the Earth's motion give Delhi both day and night?
options: Delhi turns toward and away from the Sun
The Sun circles Delhi once each day
The Moon covers the Sun after sunset
The Sun hides behind the Earth at night
items.explain: The Earth spins on its axis, so Delhi faces the Sun by day and faces away at night.

wrong.why: thinks the Sun moves around the Earth daily
thinks the Moon covers the Sun at night
repeats Aarav's idea that the Sun hides behind Earth

items.evidence: Dadu shook his head, explaining that seasons change due to the Earth's tilt and its revolution around the Sun, not because of the distance.
items.q: The Earth moves nearer the Sun in its orbit. Will that make Delhi hot?
options: No, tilt and orbit cause the seasons
Yes, being nearer always brings summer
Yes, but only when the axis is straight
No, the Earth stops spinning when nearer
items.explain: Seasons come from the Earth's tilt and revolution, not from its distance from the Sun.

wrong.why: thinks summer comes from being closer to the Sun
thinks the axis is straight, not tilted
invents a link between distance and spinning

items.evidence: To keep our calendar accurate, we add an extra day to February every four years, which we call a leap year.
items.q: Why do we add an extra day to February every four years?
options: To keep the calendar matching the Earth's orbit
To make February as long as other months
To match the Earth's spin of one day
To make up for a year of 365 days
items.explain: The Earth takes about 365 and a quarter days to orbit, so the extra day keeps the calendar accurate.

wrong.why: thinks the aim is to even out month lengths
mixes up the one-day spin with the year-long orbit
thinks a leap year has 365 days
